To: DHS Leadership, Office of Employee Culture, Administration Equity Directors, Equity Specialists, and Interested Parties
From: Equity & Inclusion Operations Consultant, Disability Services Division
Subject: Partnership Framework: Embedding Equity in the Current DHS Structure Through the One DHS People, Access and Culture Program

---

Introduction: Adapting to the New DHS Reality

This framework reflects the significant structural changes at the Minnesota Department of Human Services (DHS). Following the 2023-2024 agency realignment, DHS has undergone a substantial transformation. Direct Care and Treatment (DCT) has transitioned to the Minnesota Department of Health (MDH), and Children and Family Services has moved to the newly created Department of Children, Youth, and Families (DCYF).

This restructuring presents both a challenge and an opportunity. The challenge is that DHS must redefine its identity and operational focus. The opportunity is that we can build equity into the new DHS from the ground up, rather than retrofitting it onto legacy systems.

DHS now serves as the central hub for Minnesota's public health insurance programs, economic assistance, disability services, aging services, and behavioral health. With a budget still in the tens of billions and serving over one million Minnesotans, the equity mandate remains urgent.

This framework focuses on the current DHS portfolio, identifying where equity operations must be embedded now. It is offered in partnership with the Office of Employee Culture, Administration Equity Directors, Equity Specialists, and all interested parties as part of the One DHS People, Access and Culture Program.

This is not a decision memo. It is an invitation to partnership.

---

Phase 1: Operational Diagnosis & Integration (Months 1-3)

The following divisions represent the highest leverage points for systemic equity work within the restructured DHS. Each section outlines suggested actions and tools we can use together.

---

1. Health Care Administration (Medicaid / Medical Assistance / MinnesotaCare)

The Operational Pain Point: Health Care Administration (HCA) is now the undisputed engine of DHS. It administers Medical Assistance (MA), MinnesotaCare, and related programs. Health disparities in Minnesota are stark—Black, Indigenous, and communities of color experience significantly worse health outcomes, maternal morbidity, and chronic disease rates. These inequities are not accidents; they are baked into reimbursement rates, network adequacy standards, and care delivery models.

Suggested Actions & Tools

1.1 Managed Care Contract Redesign

· Action: Partner with HCA leadership and Equity Directors to review current contracts with Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) and county-based purchasing plans. Move beyond "diversity, equity, and inclusion plan" boilerplate language to binding performance-based equity metrics.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Contract Language Library—a searchable digital collection of model equity clauses for RFPs, contracts, and MOUs that includes disaggregated data reporting requirements, community engagement mandates, workforce equity standards, and financial consequences for non-performance. This tool can be used to insert binding requirements for MCOs to report on maternal and infant health outcomes by race and geography, access to primary care for BIPOC enrollees, and wait times for mental health and substance use disorder treatment by race, language, and disability status.

1.2 Payment Reform for Equity

· Action: Partner with the HCA actuarial team and Equity Specialists to analyze how current fee-for-service and value-based payment models may inadvertently disadvantage providers serving high-need, under-resourced communities.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Funding Equity Mapping Tool—an interactive data visualization resource used to overlay demographic data with funding distribution to reveal geographic and demographic disparities in resource allocation. This tool can be used to model equity-adjusted payment rates for providers in historically redlined or underinvested areas, enhanced reimbursement for community health workers and peer support specialists, and incentives for integrated care models addressing social determinants of health.

1.3 Culturally Specific Provider Network Expansion

· Action: Work with Provider Relations and Equity Directors to identify barriers to enrollment for BIPOC-owned clinics, Indigenous healers, and immigrant-serving organizations. Streamline credentialing, offer technical assistance for billing, and create a dedicated liaison for these providers.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Provider Onboarding Gap Analysis Template—a diagnostic tool used to identify specific barriers preventing culturally specific organizations from becoming DHS-certified providers, paired with a Technical Assistance Curriculum tailored to community-based organizations. This tool can be used to streamline credentialing and build billing capacity for underserved providers.

---

2. Disability Services and Aging

The Operational Pain Point: With the transition of DCT to MDH, DHS retains responsibility for disability waiver administration, home and community-based services (HCBS), and aging services. The direct care workforce crisis remains acute. BIPOC and immigrant workers are overrepresented in these low-wage, high-burnout positions, while BIPOC and Indigenous service recipients often face barriers to accessing culturally appropriate care and services.

Suggested Actions & Tools

2.1 Waiver Equity Analysis

· Action: Partner with Disability Services Division leadership and the Data Analytics Unit to conduct a disaggregated analysis of who is receiving services under the Brain Injury (BI), Community Access for Disability Inclusion (CADI), Community Alternative Care (CAC), and Developmental Disabilities (DD) waivers.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Lifecycle Equity Dashboard—an interactive data visualization template that can be adapted to track waiver enrollment, application and approval rates by race, ethnicity, language, and geography, the geographic distribution of service providers against BIPOC population density, and differences in service utilization rates and types of services accessed. This tool can be used to identify where eligible individuals are falling through the cracks or receiving lower-quality services based on identity or location.

2.2 Direct Support Professional (DSP) Equity Strategy

· Action: Work with the Disability Services Division and HR Business Partners to analyze wage and hour data for DSPs, develop career lattice pathways from DSP to Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) or other advanced roles, and partner with community colleges and workforce development programs to create accessible training pipelines.
· A Tool We Can Use: A DSP Workforce Equity Dashboard—an interactive data visualization template used to visualize wage, hour, and advancement disparities for direct care workers by race, ethnicity, immigration status, and geography. This tool can be used to identify disparities in scheduling, overtime, and benefits access and to advocate for loan forgiveness and tuition reimbursement for BIPOC and immigrant DSPs.

2.3 Aging Services Equity

· Action: Partner with Aging Services leadership and Equity Directors to assess current Older Americans Act and state-funded service delivery models to identify gaps in culturally specific dementia care, end-of-life planning, and caregiver support for immigrant and BIPOC communities.
· A Tool We Can Use: An Equity Impact Assessment Toolkit—a set of resources including a user-friendly template, scoring rubric, and decision-tree flowchart that can be used to evaluate the equity implications of proposed changes to aging services delivery models and recommend culturally responsive program expansions.

---

3. Economic Assistance and Employment Services (SNAP / MFIP / General Assistance)

The Operational Pain Point: Economic assistance programs are the front door to DHS for many low-income families. Administrative burden—the "time tax" of complex applications, verification requirements, and recertification processes—disproportionately impacts single parents, people with limited English proficiency, and individuals with disabilities. The "benefits cliff" (losing benefits when income increases slightly) traps families in poverty.

Suggested Actions & Tools

3.1 Administrative Burden Reduction Initiative

· Action: Partner with Economic Assistance leadership and Equity Specialists to lead a comprehensive "paperwork audit" of SNAP, MFIP, and General Assistance (GA) applications. Map every step in the application and recertification process, identify which steps cause the highest rates of application abandonment, simplify forms to a 6th-grade reading level, and eliminate redundant verification requirements.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Burden Mapping Template—a step-by-step visual mapping tool used to document every client touchpoint in an application or renewal process, paired with a Simplification Checklist that provides plain-language standards and redundancy elimination guidelines. This tool can be used to reduce client burden and expand the use of data-sharing agreements with other state agencies.

3.2 Language Access Overhaul

· Action: Partner with Economic Assistance and the Office of Employee Culture to standardize language access protocols across all Economic Assistance touchpoints, ensuring that a client's preferred language follows them through the entire eligibility determination and case management lifecycle.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Language Access Protocol Toolkit—a comprehensive resource containing staff training modules, signage templates, data field specifications for tracking language preference, and a vendor quality scorecard for evaluating translation and interpretation services. This tool can be used to ensure no client receives fragmented or English-only communications.

3.3 Benefits Cliff Mitigation

· Action: Partner with Economic Assistance leadership to model the impact of current income thresholds and phase-out rates. Explore policy options such as gradual benefit reduction, extended transitional benefits for families exiting MFIP, and increased asset limits.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Funding Equity Mapping Tool—an interactive data visualization resource used to model the impact of different policy scenarios on family economic stability. This tool can be used to advocate for policy changes that allow families to build savings without losing eligibility.

---

4. Behavioral Health and Substance Use Services

The Operational Pain Point: DHS is a major funder and regulator of behavioral health services in Minnesota. Access to mental health and substance use disorder treatment is deeply inequitable. BIPOC communities face higher rates of unmet mental health need, are more likely to be diagnosed with severe mental illness, and are less likely to receive culturally responsive care. The criminalization of substance use and mental illness disproportionately impacts Black and Indigenous communities.

Suggested Actions & Tools

4.1 Culturally Specific Provider Infrastructure

· Action: Partner with Behavioral Health leadership and Equity Directors to assess the current network of behavioral health providers contracted with DHS. Identify geographic and cultural deserts where BIPOC and Indigenous communities lack access to providers who share their identity and lived experience. Develop a targeted capacity-building strategy to support community-based organizations in becoming Medicaid-certified behavioral health providers.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Provider Onboarding Gap Analysis Template—a diagnostic tool used to identify specific barriers preventing culturally specific organizations from becoming DHS-certified providers, paired with a Technical Assistance Curriculum tailored to community-based organizations. This tool can be used to build capacity in underserved communities.

4.2 Peer Support Expansion

· Action: Partner with Behavioral Health leadership to review DHS's current peer support credentialing and reimbursement policies to identify barriers to entry and advocate for expanded coverage of peer support services in Medical Assistance.
· A Tool We Can Use: An Equity Impact Assessment Toolkit—a set of resources including a user-friendly template, scoring rubric, and decision-tree flowchart that can be used to evaluate the equity implications of current credentialing and reimbursement policies and identify where changes are needed.

4.3 Crisis Response Equity

· Action: Partner with Behavioral Health leadership and the Data Analytics Unit to analyze call volume, response times, and outcome data for the 988 crisis line and mobile crisis response teams by race, geography, and language to ensure that BIPOC communities are not being underserved or over-criminalized in crisis situations.
· A Tool We Can Use: An Equity Accountability Dashboard—a public-facing progress tracker with pre-designed wireframes, indicator definitions, and a reporting calendar template. This tool can be used to monitor crisis response equity and report findings to the legislature and the public.

---

Immediate Next Steps (The First 90 Days)

To achieve the above, the following immediate actions are suggested in partnership with the One DHS People, Access and Culture Program:

1. Stakeholder Listening Tour: Convene structured listening sessions with DHS division leaders, frontline staff, county partners, Tribal nations, and community-based organizations to ground our analysis in lived reality, not just data reports.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Community Co-Design Playbook—a practical guide that includes recruitment strategies, compensation guidelines, facilitation agendas, and feedback loop mechanisms for meaningfully engaging community members and staff as partners.
2. Data Infrastructure Audit: Meet with the DHS Data Analytics Unit to assess current data collection, disaggregation, and reporting capabilities. Identify what data is available, what is missing, and what is needed to measure equity outcomes effectively.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Data Governance for Equity Framework—a structured guide that addresses privacy considerations, tribal data sovereignty, and responsible use protocols, along with templates for data-sharing agreements with counties, tribes, and community partners.
3. Contract Language Review: Initiate a review of all active DHS contracts with managed care organizations, county partners, and service providers to identify existing equity language and gaps.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Contract Language Library—a searchable digital collection of model equity clauses for RFPs, contracts, and MOUs that can be used to compare existing contract language against best practice standards.
4. Equity Impact Assessment Adaptation: Adapt the Equity Impact Assessment tool to the new DHS structure. Before any new policy, waiver amendment, or system change is approved, it must be screened for equity impact: Who will this negatively impact? What data informed this decision? Have affected communities been consulted?
· A Tool We Can Use: An Equity Impact Assessment Toolkit—a set of resources including a user-friendly template, scoring rubric, and decision-tree flowchart that can be used to evaluate the equity implications of proposed changes before they are approved.
5. Community Co-Design Protocol: Establish a formal protocol for compensating community members with lived experience (Medicaid enrollees, disability waiver recipients, SNAP participants) for their time consulting on DHS operations. Move from passive listening to active partnership.
· A Tool We Can Use: A Community Co-Design Playbook—a practical guide that includes recruitment strategies, compensation guidelines, facilitation agendas, and feedback loop mechanisms for meaningfully engaging community members as design partners.

---

Conclusion: A Shared Journey Across One DHS

This framework is not mine to own. It is a partnership proposal—an offering of tools, frameworks, and operational expertise to the Office of Employee Culture, the Equity Directors, the Equity Specialists, and all interested parties who carry the daily weight of this work across every DHS administration.

As a staff member of the Disability Services Division, I bring a specific perspective—disability equity—to this collective effort. But the work of equity is not confined to any single division, administration, or office. It is the work of One DHS.

Together, we can build a Department of Human Services where equity is not a program, but the operating system of everything we do—from how we treat our employees to how we serve the people of Minnesota.

This is our shared work. I am ready to begin.

Respectfully submitted,

The Equity & Inclusion Operations Consultant
Disability Services Division
Aging and Disability Services Administration
Minnesota Department of Human Services
In Partnership with the One DHS People, Access and Culture Program
